Handmaid
HAND-mayd
n.
Hand + maid; renders the Hebrew ’āmāh (female servant, handmaid) and shiphchāh (maidservant); and the Greek doulē (female servant, bondwoman).

📖 Biblical Definition

Handmaid in Scripture is the title of a female servant—literal in many uses, but supremely transferred as a self-designation by several great female saints to set forth their relation to the LORD whom they served. The most famous use is Mary’s at the annunciation: when Gabriel announces that she shall conceive and bear the Son of the Highest, her response is one of the most theologically weighty sentences in Scripture: and Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word (Luke 1:38). Mary names herself doulē kuriou—female bondservant of the Lord—and submits unconditionally to His word. The Magnificat takes up the theme: my soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour. For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden (Luke 1:46-48). The handmaid title is therefore Mary’s settled self-understanding before God: not mother of God chiefly (though the term has its proper place in confessing the incarnation), not queen of heaven (a title Scripture nowhere applies to her), but handmaid of the Lord—the servant who receives what God appoints and lives for His purposes. Hannah uses the same title in her great prayer: O LORD of hosts, if thou wilt indeed look on the affliction of thine handmaid, and remember me, and not forget thine handmaid, but wilt give unto thine handmaid a man child, then I will give him unto the LORD all the days of his life (1 Sam 1:11). Ruth uses it of herself before Boaz (Ruth 3:9). Abigail uses it before David repeatedly (1 Sam 25:24-31). The handmaid title is therefore the great female-saint self-designation in Scripture, paralleling the masculine servant or bondservant (doulos) by which Paul and other apostles identify themselves. Its key marks are several. It is a posture of glad submission to God’s appointments; it is the inward disposition of one who has accepted her place under God and receives what He sends without quarrel; it is the freedom from self-importance that makes the handmaid available for whatever God assigns; and it is, in the cases of Mary, Hannah, Ruth, and Abigail, the precise inward disposition God blessed and used to accomplish some of the most consequential moves in redemptive history. The handmaid is not a diminished or oppressed figure in Scripture; she is the freed soul, having submitted her will to God’s, who is now used by Him in proportion to her availability.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HANDMAID as a maid that waits at hand; a female servant or attendant; in scripture, the self-designation by which Mary, Hannah, Ruth, Abigail, and other female saints name their relation to the LORD they serve.

expand to see more

HANDMAID, n. — A maid that waits at hand; a female servant or attendant. Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word (Luke 1:38).

MAIDSERVANT, n. — A female servant; especially, one who attends at the table or in domestic offices.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 1:38 — "And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her."

Luke 1:46-48 — "And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour. For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden..."

1 Samuel 1:11 — "And she vowed a vow, and said, O LORD of hosts, if thou wilt indeed look on the affliction of thine handmaid, and remember me, and not forget thine handmaid..."

Acts 2:18 — "And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The handmaid title is corrupted, on one side, by the cultural rejection of servant language as inherently demeaning, against the apostles’ and great female saints’ own self-designation—and on the other by the Marian-elevation traditions that have replaced Mary’s own settled self-understanding as handmaid with titles she neither claimed nor accepted (queen of heaven, mediatrix, co-redemptrix).

expand to see more

The cultural rejection of servant language as inherently demeaning is one corruption of the handmaid title. The contemporary register treats any submission as oppression, any acceptance of a place under another as inauthenticity, any glad self-designation as servant or handmaid as evidence of unhealthy patterning. Scripture refuses the framing. Mary’s behold the handmaid of the Lord is the celebrated inward disposition that opens her to bear the Savior of the world; Hannah’s self-designation as handmaid is the disposition the LORD honors with Samuel’s birth and Israel’s prophetic-political renewal; Paul’s identification of himself as doulos Christou (slave of Christ) opens nearly every epistle. The biblical pattern is that the freed soul gladly takes the lower seat, identifies as servant of the LORD, and finds in that very identification the freedom and the usefulness that no self-elevation can produce. Recover the doctrine, and the handmaid title recovers its dignity: not oppression-language but freedom-language.

The opposite corruption, more visible in some Christian traditions, is the Marian-elevation that has replaced Mary’s own settled self-understanding as handmaid with titles she neither claimed nor accepted. The biblical Mary calls herself handmaid; she rejoices in God her Savior (Luke 1:47), a title that confesses her need of salvation alongside every other sinner; she points the wedding-servants to her Son with the words whatsoever he saith unto you, do it (John 2:5); and after Pentecost she largely disappears from the narrative as the apostles get on with the gospel mission. The medieval and modern elevations of Mary to queen of heaven, mediatrix, co-redemptrix, sinless conception, and bodily assumption are not what Mary said about herself and not what Scripture says about her. Recover the biblical Mary, and recover also the dignity of the handmaid title she bore: a real woman, of low estate by her own account, who submitted gladly to God’s appointment, bore the Son of the Highest, pointed others to Him, and rejoiced in Him as her Savior. The handmaid title is not a diminishment; it is the very disposition God Himself honored by giving her the highest privilege Scripture records of any human creature.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ’āmāh (female servant, handmaid) and shiphchāh (maidservant); Greek doulē (female bondservant—Mary’s self-designation in Luke 1:38, 48; Acts 2:18)—the freed-soul disposition of glad submission to God’s appointments, supreme self-designation of Mary, Hannah, Ruth, and Abigail.

expand to see more

Hebrew ’āmāh (H519) — female servant, handmaid (Hannah, 1 Sam 1:11; Ruth 3:9; Abigail 1 Sam 25:24).

Hebrew shiphchāh (H8198) — maidservant.

Greek doulē (G1399) — female bondservant (Luke 1:38, 48; Acts 2:18).

Greek paidiskē (G3814) — female servant, slave-girl (Acts 16:16-19 of the demoniac girl; Gal 4:22-31 of Hagar).

Usage

"Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word—Mary’s settled self-designation at the most consequential moment in redemptive history."

"Hannah, Ruth, Abigail, and Mary all use the handmaid title—the great female-saint self-designation in Scripture, parallel to the masculine servant or doulos."

"Cultural rejection of servant language and Marian-elevation traditions are opposite corruptions; biblical handmaid is the freed soul gladly submitting to God’s appointments."
